quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright by laborers.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) -- browse image-by-image.
Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

Search Sheahan and variant spellings across all Pennsylvania entries.

The 1900 US Federal Census (name-searchable) asks each foreign-born person for the year of immigration and number of years in the United States, and asks each person how many years they have been in their current county. Those answers can confirm or refute the c.1882 arrival date and supply the birthplace or country of origin, which may explain the migration corridor. Neighbors' birthplaces in the same mining community are a FAN lead: a cluster of co-migrants from the same Irish county would support chain migration over purely economic pull.

The 1910 US Federal Census (name-searchable) asks for years of immigration and years in current county, and records whether the subject is an employee or a mine worker specifically. If Michael is still in Schuylkill in 1910, a mining occupation confirmed across three census years (1882, 1900, 1910) makes occupation-driven migration far more plausible than coincidence. Neighbor enumeration also extends the FAN cluster begun in the 1900 item.

Naturalization records for Schuylkill County (browse-only, personCount 0, image group 007936750, covering 1849-1915) sometimes state the petitioner's prior county or township of residence, occupation, and witnesses — often neighbors or a sponsor from the same place of origin. If Michael naturalized in Schuylkill County, the declaration of intent or final petition may name his prior Pennsylvania county, his birthplace, and a witness who was a co-migrant, providing direct evidence about the migration chain. Browse image-by-image; the loc_001 quirk confirms these are unindexed.

Patrick Sheahan (brother, I2) is documented in Schuylkill County in 1875 with a sourced deed (Deed Book 42, p. 118 — F4/S1), showing he preceded Michael by roughly seven years. The deed image-group 007936752 (22% record-searchable) should be searched for both Patrick and Michael Sheahan: Patrick's deed may name a grantor, a witness, or adjoining owner who is a FAN member and part of the same migration network, and a later deed in Michael's name (if any) dates his settled presence independently of the census. Search the name-indexed portion first; browse for years after the index coverage ends. The loc_001 quirk notes that coal-region laborers often leased rather than purchased land, so a null result here is itself informative.

The Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records collection (name-searchable, personCount 982415) covers 1708-1985 and includes Roman Catholic parish registers — the likely denomination for an Irish immigrant named Sheahan. A baptism, marriage, or burial entry for Michael or Patrick Sheahan may name a townland or Irish county of origin, a co-sponsor from the same community, or a priest of the same national origin. The Diocese of Philadelphia (the loc_001 quirk confirms Schuylkill fell under Philadelphia until 1961) fielded Irish-born priests who sometimes recorded Irish origins in sacramental entries. An image-browse volume (007936751, 1842-1895) also exists for cases where the index misses entries; search it if the name-indexed result is thin.

Chronicling America (loc.gov/collections/chronicling-america) holds digitized issues of the Miners' Journal (Pottsville, Schuylkill County) from 1825 onward, full-text searchable. Mine accident reports, company announcements, strike coverage, and social notices often name individual miners by township and sometimes by county of origin. A search for 'Sheahan' and variants in issues from 1878-1892 may directly name Michael's mine, his hiring date, or his migration circumstances. This is the most direct external evidence for an occupation-driven reason for the move. Fallback to this item if the FamilySearch sources establish his presence but not his motive.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been located. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

Swedish marriage entries of this era frequently name the bride's home parish or father, which would directly reveal Elena's origin and confirm her father's given name as Asmund. The national Sweden, Marriages, 1630-1920 collection (1520596) is name-searchable, making this a name search on Jöns Jönsson and Elena. The loc_002 entry notes that the Västra Karaby volumes on FamilySearch (image groups 004523021, 004523018) are browse-only (personCount 0) and 0% indexed, so if the national index yields no hit, a browse of those volumes for December 1712 is the fallback. Elena is a known variant of Helena, Elin and Ellen per the Sweden Naming Customs wiki page, so all forms should be tried.

If the national marriage index returns no result, the Västra Karaby register volumes on FamilySearch (image groups 004523021 and 004523018, each 0% indexed) hold the only surviving copies of the marriage register from 1688 onward. These are browse-only (personCount 0). Browsing to December 1712 would yield the original marriage entry, which in Swedish Lutheran practice names the groom's and bride's parishes of origin and the bride's father — the most direct route to Elena's birthplace and parentage. The loc_002 entry notes that one coverage row on 004523021 reads 1662–1850. This item is a fallback for the national index search in item 1.

Elena's patronym 'Asmundsdotter' establishes that her father was named Asmund — an uncommon name in Skåne. The national Sweden, Baptisms, 1611–1920 collection (1520594) is name-searchable, so a search for 'Elena' (and variants Helena, Elin, Ellen) daughter of a father named 'Asmund' across Malmöhus county for c. 1680–1700 could directly return her baptism entry and identify the parish. The loc_001 and loc_002 entries note that Skåne was Danish until 1658, so pre-1688 coverage is partial; the Barsebäck and Västra Karaby registers do not begin until 1688, but other Malmöhus parishes may have earlier coverage. This search casts the net county-wide because Elena's birth parish is the unknown.

Elena's son Asmund Jönsson was christened in Barsebäck on 11 September 1718 and died there on 4 February 1768, suggesting the family resided in Barsebäck after the marriage. Elena's own burial entry in the Barsebäck register — volume image groups 004514823 and 004514824, browse-only (personCount 0) — may name her age at death, her home parish of origin, or her father's name. Because Elena's birth date is unknown, this item is dated from after the marriage to c. 1760 (the outer plausible bound for her death, given a marriage in 1712). The loc_001 entry notes the Barsebäck register begins 1648 and is 0% indexed. The national Sweden, Burials, 1649–1920 (1520597) is name-searchable and should be tried first; a browse of the Barsebäck volumes is the fallback. Skipping this item would leave an important end-of-life record unchecked.

This is the browse fallback for item 4 if the national Burials index returns no hit for Elena. The Barsebäck register volumes on FamilySearch (image groups 004514823 and 004514824) are browse-only (personCount 0) and cover 1648–1861 per the loc_001 quirks entry. Browsing the burial register for the years 1713–1760 would catch Elena's burial entry if she died in or near Barsebäck, and such entries in this era commonly name the deceased's age or former parish.

The loc_002 entry records that household tax lists (mantalslängder) survive for Harjager härad from 1658 and are held by Riksarkivet (https://sok.riksarkivet.se/mantalslangder). A male householder named 'Asmund' appearing in Harjager härad before 1712 — with a daughter of Elena's approximate age — would identify Elena's father and home household before the marriage. Because Elena's birth is estimated c. 1680–1695, the search window for an 'Asmund' householder is set to 1658–1715 (the period he was plausibly a household head whose daughter was approaching marriage age). A hit where both names appear in the same entry or on the same page could place Elena as a daughter of Asmund in a specific parish. The co-occurrence should be run unscoped (not limited to a single collection id) to catch all Malmöhus parish volumes. Per the Sweden Naming Customs wiki page, the suffix '-dotter' was frequently abbreviated as d., dr., dtr., so search variants of the suffix as well.

FAN item: the siblings of Elena Asmundsdotter — other children of Asmund — would appear in the baptism register of whichever Malmöhus parish the family lived in. The national Sweden, Marriages, 1630-1920 collection (1520596) is name-searchable, making this a name search on Jöns Jönsson and Elena. The loc_002 entry notes that the Västra Karaby volumes on FamilySearch (image groups 004523021, 004523018) are browse-only (personCount 0) and 0% indexed, so if the national index yields no hit, a browse of those volumes for December 1712 is the fallback. If the national marriage index returns no result, the Västra Karaby register volumes on FamilySearch (image groups 004523021 and 004523018, each 0% indexed) hold the only surviving copies of the marriage register from 1688 onward. These are browse-only (personCount 0). Browsing to December 1712 would yield the original marriage entry, which in Swedish Lutheran practice names the groom's and bride's parishes of origin and the bride's father — the most direct route to Elena's birthplace and parentage. The loc_002 entry notes that one coverage row on 004523021 reads 1662–1850. This item is a fallback for the national index search in item 1.

Elena's patronym 'Asmundsdotter' establishes that her father was named Asmund — an uncommon name in Skåne. The national Sweden, Baptisms, 1611–1920 collection (1520594) is name-searchable, so a search for 'Elena' (and variants Helena, Elin, Ellen) daughter of a father named 'Asmund' across Malmöhus county for c. 1680–1700 could directly return her baptism entry and identify the parish. This search casts the net county-wide because Elena's birth parish is the unknown.

Elena's son Asmund Jönsson was christened in Barsebäck on 11 September 1718 and died there on 4 February 1768, suggesting the family resided in Barsebäck after the marriage. Elena's own burial entry in the Barsebäck register — volume image groups 004514823 and 004514824, browse-only (personCount 0) — may name her age at death, her home parish of origin, or her father's name. quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright by laborers.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) -- browse image-by-image.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.
